contributions of this work are high quality open source images, reasonable
performance on RFS Dataset and validation of super pixel delimiting masks as a
form of data augmentation.

these categories has been independently addressed by various researchers to
improve visibility and ensure road safety. However, these segments have
received different attention from researchers with respect to availability of
data, visibility impact on road and research popularity. For example, rain
classification has received most of the attention due to availability of large
amount of data and advance in technology. On the other side, fog classification
has received least attention due to less availability of data. Therefore, there
is a need for a comprehensive system which includes three primary classes i.e

an approach to improving
the representation of convection in weather and climate models. This is an
attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No
further modelling of sub-filter variability is included. We then apply this
model to Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, showing that, with minimal closures,
the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of
magnitude of buoyancy forcing (Ra). This suggests that even a very simple
two-fluid model can accurately capture the dominant coherent overturning
structures of convection.
  In contrast, a simple one-fluid model closes the mean buoyancy force on a
fictitious "mean fluid". As such it fails to predict the correct scaling of the
heat flux [Nu does not scale as Ra$^{1/2}$], unless significant mixing between
the two fluids is assumed for the mean fluid. This has implications for the
development of multi-fluid convection schemes: the falling fluid will be
responsible for the drying of the mid-levels in tropical regions, and will
impact on the formation of cloud and precipitation.
  Finally, we suggest a closure for the flux of mass from the rising to the
falling fluid, based on the sub-filter variability of the square of the
difference between their weights. This is then shown to lead to a correct
scaling of the mass flux between the two fluids.

Twitter provides organizations and
individuals an effective way to monitor public emotions towards them and their
competitors. As a result, sentiment analysis has become an important and
challenging task. In this work, we have collected seven publicly available and
manually annotated twitter sentiment datasets. We create a new training and
testing dataset from the collected datasets. We develop an LSTM model to
classify sentiment of a tweet and evaluate the model with the new dataset.
Although the performance is good, we notice that the model has difficulty in
classifying the neutral tweets. We think one of the reasons is that the
category of "neutral" in twitter sentiment generally implies the tweet is
balanced which means it may have both positive and negative emotions. To make the
model learn to classify the balanced emotions in the neutral tweets, we propose
a new dataset with balanced emotions labeled as both positive and negative.
We add the new dataset to the original dataset and retrain a new model. The new
model performs better than the original model in classifying the neutral tweets.
Our experiments demonstrate that our method can make the model to learn to
classify the balanced emotions in the neutral tweets.
  Which news source is trustworthy? People often check the credibility of news
from the home page of the news source. However, most home pages do not provide
any information about their credibility certification. How do people then make
such judgments? We find that people make such decisions by looking at,
respectively, the logos and the names of the news websites. This indicates that
people rely on automatic credibility certification provided by the layout of
the web pages. We then ask the important question: Can machines learn to
recognize the layout patterns that indicate the credibility of a news source?
Although there is no explicit empirical evidence, we hypothesize that web
entities related to credibility (ECWs) are the key. We observe that ECWs have
consistent layouts. They are more likely to exist in famous news sources. The
more ECWs a news website has, the more likely the website is a reliable one.
This indicates BCWs can serve as a semi-automatic credibility certification
scheme from the perspective of machines. To verify our hypothesis, we propose a
novel method named ECW-Detector. It uses learning to find ECWs, which are then
counted to determine the reliability of the website. Our experiments on real
webpages indicate that ECW-Detector is much better than previous schemes.

However, building a chat system is not scalable since it often requires a
considerable volume of human-human dialogue data, especially when enforcing
features such as persona, style, or safety. In this work, we study the
challenge of imposing roles on open-domain dialogue systems, with the goal of
making the systems maintain consistent roles while conversing naturally with
humans. To accomplish this, the system must satisfy a role specification that
includes certain conditions on the stated features as well as a system policy
on whether or not certain types of utterances are allowed. For this, we propose
an efficient data collection framework leveraging in-context few-shot learning
of large-scale language models for building role-satisfying dialogue dataset
from scratch. We then compare various architectures for open-domain dialogue
systems in terms of meeting role specifications while maintaining
conversational abilities. Automatic and human evaluations show that our models
return few out-of-bounds utterances, while maintaining an 18% improvement in
response quality over a baseline model that is trained with all possible
possible next-response predictions at each time step. We release a English
dialogue dataset, named DialRole, which includes four subdatasets, each with a
distinct role specification, to aid future research on dialogue policy
evaluation and consumption.

The efficacies of pesticide
treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.
  Our results show that this method is useful in ranking pesticide treatments
when trials are not fully replicated. The results also show that the disease
pressure affects the strawberry yield and profit in Florida. The proposed
methodology provides farmers and extension agents with more efficient
information to select the best management practice considering the potential
yield and profit, as well as the risk associated with these outcomes.
Moreover, management practices that are efficient in terms of profit and
yield are identified. Finally, the efficiency of a management practice can be
considered as being suitable for a given level of disease pressure.
  Keywords: Certainty equivalents, disease pressure, strawberry, stochastic
efficiency.

cliques, namely, the decision version of the minimum vertex-deletable clique
problem. A clique in a graph G = (V, E) is a subset of vertices of size p such
that all pairs of vertices in it are adjacent. When we delete a vertex from G we
remove it together with all edges in which it participates. A vertex-deletable
clique is a clique such that after deleting one of its vertices it becomes a
clique in an auxiliary graph which does not contain isolated vertices. The
minimum vertex-deletable clique problem is to find among all vertex-deletable
cliques of a given graph G the one with the minimum number of vertices. The
decision version of this problem is to determine whether such a clique exists in
G which contains at least k vertices. We show that the decision version of this
problem is NP-complete.

role of the Web as a driver of polarization. In order to further our
understanding of the factors behind online polarization, in the present work we
collect and analyze Web browsing histories of tens of thousands of users

visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show
that such preferences hold at the individual as well as the population level,
as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by
the considered news domains, finding strong evidence of polarization in
partisan browsing habits beyond that which can be explained by the hyperlink
structure of the Web.

incorporate other dimensions; examining the role of algorithmic change; and
investigating the relationship between online polarization and real-world

QCD axion sector can account for neutrino oscillations, dark matter and baryon
asymmetry; at the same time, it solves the strong CP problem, stabilizes the
electroweak vacuum and can implement critical Higgs inflation (satisfying all
current observational bounds). We perform here a general analysis of dark
matter (DM) in such a model, which we call the $a\nu$MSM. Although critical
Higgs inflation features a (quasi) inflection point of the inflaton potential
we show that DM cannot receive a contribution from primordial black holes in
the $a\nu$MSM. This leads to a multicomponent axion-sterile-neutrino DM and
allows us to relate the axion parameters, such as the axion decay constant, to
the neutrino parameters. We include several DM production mechanisms: the axion
production via misalignment and decay of topological defects as well as the
sterile-neutrino production through the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms
and in the recently proposed CPT-symmetric universe.
  Combining the constraints from all DM experiments we derive allowed ranges
for the axion parameters leading to a DM density in the $a\nu$MSM that can be
accounted for by the axion-sterile-neutrino subsystem alone. We also impose
new bounds on the sterile-neutrino parameters, which are crucial to relate
these to the axion parameters. We further exploit the DM results to constrain
the cosmologically relevant range of the neutrinoless double beta decay
efficiency in the $a\nu$MSM, which can be tested in ongoing and future
experiments.
  Finally, we present a brief discussion on the indirect searches for DM with
the characteristic signature of the $a\nu$MSM, namely a sterile-neutrino
component. We show that the future experiments AMPEX and PROZEN can improve
the constraints on the sterile-neutrino parameters by four orders of magnitude
and indicate that light sterile neutrinos may already be visible in the
published data of the direct detection experiments or may be discovered in the
near future.
  We have not included the lower limits on the sterile-neutrino mass, which
may be derived from leptogenesis and from requiring that the $a\nu$MSM has a
minimum number of physical parameters.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.
  We propose an auxiliary task of predicting crisp boundaries and a mechanism to
gate the feature maps with the boundary information. We evaluate the efficacy of
the proposed EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available
datasets, BraTS 19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation.
We demonstrate how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation
accuracy and generalization performance.

generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists and practitioners are difficult to identify implicit biases
in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable unbias test datasets to valid
models. To tackle this issue, we first define the data intrinsic bias
attribute, and then propose a novel bias identification framework for medical
image datasets. The framework contains two major components, KlotskiNet and
Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis(bdda), where KlostkiNet is to build the
mapping which makes backgrounds to distinguish positive and negative samples
and bdda provides a theoretical solution on determining bias attributes.
Experimental results on three datasets show the effectiveness of the bias
attributes discovered by the framework.
  When validating a medical image analysis application, usually some biases
existing in the training dataset will be learned by the model, and then
degrade the performance on the test data. To tackle this problem, researchers
and scientists have to identify the biases in the dataset so as to find proper
solutions. However, in practice, it is a difficult task for scientists to find
implicit biases in the dataset. To solve this problem, we propose a framework
containing two key components: attribute definition and bias identification.
With respect to attribute definition, we first give a definition of data
intrinsic bias attribute based on the feature distribution difference between
samples of different labels. Then our novel framework is developed to determine
the attributes according to the definition. Experimental results on three
datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the attributes discovered by our
framework.

low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume that the degree distributions of
the two ends of a randomly selected edge are independent. In the paper, we take
one step further and consider ensembles of LDPC codes with degree-degree
correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation
could improve the maximum tolerable erasure probability. Moreover, increasing
the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error
protection (UEP) design.
  Further, we exploit the system of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes to design
a novel degree-design method for constructing LDPC codes with superior
unequal error protection (UEP) performance. By tuning the degree-degree
correlation values wisely according to the proposed method, one could obtain
LDPC codes that perform better than the traditional degree-design method used in
designing UEP codes. Numerical results show that our method could be used to
design UEP codes with very large block-lengths.
  In summary, this paper proposes two methods to construct degree-degree
correlated LDPC codes, derives the corresponding density evolution equations,
and shows the improved unequal error protection (UEP) performance of LDPC codes
with positive degree-degree correlation and the superior UEP design of a new
degree-design method which can utilize the degree-degree correlation.

unified framework, density evolution, unequal error protection (UEP), degree

fundamental role on dynamical processes evolving on heterogeneous networks.
These localization analyses are frequently grounded, for example, on
eigenvectors of adjacency or non-backtracking matrices which emerge in theories
of dynamic processes near to an active to inactive transition. We advance in
this problem gauging nodal activity to quantify the localization in dynamical
processes on networks whether they are near to a transition or not. The method
is generic and applicable to theory, stochastic simulations, and real data. We
investigate spreading processes on a wide spectrum of networks, both
analytically and numerically, showing that nodal activity can present complex
patterns depending on the network structure. Using annealed networks we show
that a localized state at the transition and an endemic phase just above it are
not incompatible features of a spreading process. We also report that epidemic
prevalence near to the transition is determined by the delocalized component of
the network even when the analysis of the inverse participation ratio indicates
a localized activity. Also, dynamical processes with distinct critical
exponents can be described by the same localization pattern. Turning to
quenched networks, a more complex picture, depending on the type of activation
and on the range of degree exponent, is observed and discussed. Our work paves
an important path for investigation of localized activity in spreading and
other processes on networks.
  Furthermore, we investigate the role of localization for the spread of an
immunized individual into a population without immunity. We analyze both
analytically and numerically the relevant nodal activity at initialization and
its evolution during the spreading process. We find that a localized activity
at initialization together with a high connectivity function for the network
predict the number of infected individuals after the contact between the
immunized individual and the network. Moreover, we show that the localization
pattern is determined by the degree correlation of the network. Our results
provide important insights on the role of delocalized and localized regions in
a network for the spread of an immunized individual into a population without
immunity.
  Finally, we investigate how the number of individuals aware of a social
phenomenon, e.g. a riot, in a network is determined by the degree of localization
of the underlying spreading process. We find that a localization pattern

methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. This indicates
that without nodal-level data, many of these measures are not suitable for
quantifying polarization and distinguishing actual polarization from the noise
introduced by high-degree outliers. This is particularly important for
researchers to be aware of when studying polarization in large-scale networks.

polarization scores. They showed that only one of the methods they analyzed

to testing of
programs. Their combination is intended to lead to benefits in reliable program
development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing is
intended to serve as the specification of a testing environment, included as
the last stage of a toolchain that assists professional programmers, amateurs,
and students of Computer Science. The testing environment includes an automated
algorithm which locates errors in a test that has been run, and assists in
correcting them. It does this by displaying, on a monitor screen, a stick
diagram of causal chains in the execution of the program under test. The
diagram can then be navigated backwards in the familiar style of a satnav
following roads on a map. This will reveal selections of places at which the
program should be modified to remove the error.
  We give an overview of the underlying theory of causal dynamic systems,
introduce a simple programming language, and illustrate the use of the testing
environment.
  The development of a testing environment is intended to lead to improvements
in teaching programming, so we include material suitable for inclusion in
lessons for students.
  Professional programmers will welcome the inclusion of comments on locations
in the test program where their program can be made more efficient while
preserving correctness.
  We illustrate the use of our testing environment in testing two programs,
one for calculating the median of a sequence of numbers, and one for printing
and evaluating a mathematical expression. We show how it helps in testing the
program that we present to solve the classic two-phase commit problem. This
program has been verified correct by our Viper prover, and any errors discovered
by testing should lead to improvements in the verification environment.

and we show how the cleaner function can be used to remove errors resulting
from such garbage.

complement each other, and how a combined approach leads to a reliable program
development process.

respects the specifications laid down in the PCI-Specification.
  Finally, we discuss how our testing can be used to check that a program is
correct on all integers, a requirement often made of programs such as sorting

generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for
prompt-based task-conditioning that uses HyperNetworks. The hyper-prompts
produce task-specific hyper-parameters at inference time, which are used to
fine-tune a pre-trained language model. We show that HyperPrompt is a very
effective task-conditioning method and outperforms strong baselines on two

distribution generalization. With HyperPrompt, prompt-based task-conditioning
can be applied in a flexible way such that a single model can be used to
perform multiple tasks simply by changing the hyper-prompts. This is in
contrast to previous studies that use hyper-parametrized prompts to learn
multiple tasks in a multi-task learning setup. Overall, our experiments
demonstrate that HyperPrompt leads to excellent performance across various
text-classification tasks, using only a few additional parameters.

task-conditioning, we believe HyperPrompt to be a promising architecture for
large-scale industrial applications, where numerous tasks can be efficiently
conditioned simply by changing the hyper-prompts. With HyperPrompt, a single
model can be made to perform any task for which it has been trained, simply by
computing the task-specific hyper-prompts. This is in contrast to
Prompt-Tuning where a new model is trained from scratch for each task.

set of "probing" tasks, where each task is designed to switch on/off a

designed to produce task-specific layer activations and then used to compute a

  Our main contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm that estimates
the size of a network under the presence of a large number of Byzantine nodes.
In particular, our algorithm estimates the size of a sparse, "small-world",
expander network with up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ is
the (unknown) network size and $\delta$ can be be any arbitrarily small (but
fixed) positive constant. Our algorithm outputs a (fixed) constant factor
estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability; the correct estimate of the
network size will be known to a large fraction ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction, for
any fixed positive constant $\epsilon$) of the honest nodes. Our algorithm is
fully distributed, lightweight, and simple to implement, runs in $O(\log^3{n})$
rounds, and requires nodes to send and receive messages of only small-sized
messages per round; any node's local computation cost per round is also small.
Some of the key technical contributions of this work are (1) developing a
novel, efficient randomized protocol that achieves fast robust estimation of
the network size under the full information model (even when a large fraction
of nodes are Byzantine), and (2) showing that even a small portion of honest
nodes are enough to output a near-optimal estimate of the network size.

settings, assume that a constant fraction of nodes are honest, and are more
complex to implement. In addition, our algorithm is resilient to a large number
of Byzantine nodes, and is thus one of the first robust protocols that are
capable of even running (honestly-designed) distributed consensus protocols
(such as randomized leader election protocols) under the presence of a large
number of Byzantine nodes.

  Knowledge distillation is a popular approach for model compression. It allows
us to transform a complex model (teacher) into a simpler one (student) while
keeping most of the predictive performance. The final performance is determined
by how well the student can learn from the behavior and probability distributions
of the teacher. Thus, there are mainly two key components in knowledge
distillation algorithms: ensemble methods to combine the probabilities
generated by multi-teacher models and learning methods to utilize the label
information of data with the assistance of teacher models. Unfortunately, most
existing studies on ensemble and learning in knowledge distillation are
isolated, and there is no systematic theory to unify them. In this paper, we
focus on the pairwise ranking problem and propose Pairwise Iterative Logits
Ensemble (PILE) that simultaneously ensembles multi-teacher logits supervised by
label information in an iterative way. Compared to the baseline methods, PILE
achieves significant improvement in prediction accuracy and compression
ratio.

Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. After a sufficiently slow change from
the driver Hamiltonian to the problem Hamiltonian, we can obtain the target
ground state that corresponds to the solution. The inclusion of non-stoquastic
terms in the driver Hamiltonian is believed to enhance the efficiency of the

we present examples showing that non-stoaquastic Hamiltonians can lead to
catastrophic failure of QA, whereas a certain decoherence process can be used
to avoid such failure. More specifically, when we include anti-ferromagnetic
interactions (i.e., typical non-stoquastic terms) in the Hamiltonian, we are
unable to prepare the target ground state even with an infinitely long
annealing time for some specific cases. In our example, owing to a symmetry,
the Hamiltonian is block-diagonalized, and a crossing occurs during the QA,
which leads to a complete failure of the ground-state search. Moreover, we show
that, when we add a certain type of decoherence, we can obtain the ground state
after QA for these cases. This is because, even when symmetry exists, the
breaking of symmetry due to the decoherence leads to the desired crossing in
the energy levels. That is, a suitable decoherence can be used to break
symmetry and thus obtain the ground state of the problem Hamiltonian. This is
an example showing that decoherence, in general, is not an obstacle, but can
be a necessary tool for QA.

  When training large neural networks, memory is a major limitation for
distributing the network across multiple GPUs. Although various model-parallel
techniques have been proposed to overcome this limitation, these techniques
still require to store all layer weights in each GPU memory. In this paper, we
propose a novel approach to overcome the memory limitation in both model- and
data-parallel training schemes. The central idea is based on approximating back
propagated errors (errors to be sent to the compute node) by using a
feed-forward pattern and supplementary networks called error generators.
Thanks to the approximation, we can store only the error estimators in each
GPU memory instead of the weights. Experimental results show that our approach
achieves promising performance. For example, ResNet-50 can be trained using 8
GPU nodes with only 6MB memory consumption per node.

considering memory constraint. The central idea is to split the gradient
computation into three stages: stage1, stage2, and final. We prove that we only
need to allocate $O(1/M)$ memory in each computation stage per node when we
use $M$ cluster GPUs. We demonstrate that our approach successfully reduces
the computation time of the popular training recipes: model parallelism and
data parallelism. Experimental results show that our approach achieves
performance gain. For example, training ResNet50 can be finished in 233s when we
use 8 GPUs, while it takes 536s when we run it on a single GPU.

conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites which can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, that are difficult to
detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
determining damage shape and size in self-sensing composites. Our technique
makes use of a genetic algorithm (GA) integrated with realistic physics-based
damage models to recover precise damage shape from conductivity changes imaged
via EIT. We experimentally validate this technique on carbon nanofiber
(CNF)-modified glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates by considering
two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. Our results
show that this novel technique can accurately reconstruct multiple
through-holes with radii as small as 1.5 mm and depths up to 50% of the
laminates' thickness. Furthermore, our technique has been successfully used to
image a complex delamination defect in a previously untested laminate
configuration. We believe that this GA-based technique has promising potential to
improve the accuracy of current damage detection methods in composites and

divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a sharper decrease. There was no significant change in
engagement for both first-generation and non-first-generation students. Further

networks (GNNs) have been successfully used to learn data representations and
structures to solve classification and link prediction problems. The
applications of such methods are vast and diverse, but most of the current work
relies on the assumption of a static graph. This assumption does not hold for
many highly dynamic systems, where the underlying connectivity structure is
non-stationary and is mostly unobserved. Using a static model in these
situations may result in sub-optimal performance. In contrast, modeling changes
in graph structure with time can provide information about the system whose
applications go beyond classification. Most work of this type does not learn
effective connectivity and focuses on cross-correlation between nodes to
generate undirected graphs. An undirected graph is unable to capture direction
of an interaction which is vital in many fields, including neuroscience. To
bridge this gap, we developed dynamic effective connectivity estimation via
neural network training (DECENNT), a novel model to learn an interpretable
directed and dynamic graph induced by the downstream classification/prediction
task. DECENNT outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on five different
tasks and infers interpretable task-specific dynamic graphs. The dynamic graphs
inferred from functional neuroimaging data align well with the existing
literature and provide additional information. Additionally, the temporal
sensitivity analysis of DECENNT provides the top contributors to a task at
different time points, which can be completely distinct, demonstrating that
DECENNT captures temporal task-dependent changes in effective connectivity.
Overall, DECENNT learns a model that is able to capture temporal changes in
effective connectivity, is easy to train compared to other dynamic GNN models,
and requires only scalar task labels for training.

technological pollution and modern urbanization (e.g. migratory insects,
monarch butterflies). This diversity of locomotory behavior has inspired various
algorithmic formulations for autonomous agents in robotics and simulations.
These algorithms are designed to emulate the overall behavior of the animals
that inspire them, without a need to implement a direct biological
correspondence. Such algorithms are of particular use in search and rescue
operations, where knowledge of efficient navigation strategies can be
indispensable. In this paper, we present a survey of algorithms inspired by
animal locomotion, break down their underlying concepts and mechanisms, and
identify their animal inspirations. We also discuss their applications in
robotics and multi-agent simulations, and argue for their benefits in
engineering robustness to uncertainty and failure.

algorithm which: (1) is inspired by an animal locomotion mechanism; (2) causes

biologically-accurate algorithms, bio-inspired locomotion strategies, and
animal-based algorithms. For each category we provide an overview of its
algorithms and mechanisms, and illustrate the relationships between them. In

comparison of their searches in identical scenarios.

performance metric ($PM$) which is independent of the underlying search space.

operating multi-agent search systems. Thus, $PM$ can be used to design search
systems with greater fuel efficiency, lower communication overhead, and

deployment of HPC workloads on the best-fitting hardware. However, although
cloud and on-premise HPC systems offer similar computational resources, their
network architecture and performance may differ significantly. For example,
these systems use fundamentally different network transport and routing
protocols, which may introduce network noise that can eventually limit the
application scaling. This work analyzes network performance, scalability, and
cost of running HPC workloads on cloud systems. First, we consider latency,
bandwidth, and collective communication patterns in detailed small-scale
measurements, and then we simulate network performance at a larger scale. We
validate our approach on four popular cloud providers and three on-premise HPC
systems, showing that network (and also OS) noise can significantly impact
performance and cost both at small and large scale.
  Our study provides a scalable approach to assess the impact of the network
on cloud and on-premise HPC workloads, is free of charges for cloud providers,
and does not require any specific hardware or software in the target system.
Moreover, our code is open-source and ready to use. It can be used as a
performance-prediction tool, which can help to determine whether a cloud or
on-premise system is the best fit for any HPC workload, and also to guide
workload adaptations (e.g., changing the application communication patterns)
to fully exploit the computational and network capabilities of cloud and on-
premise HPC systems.
  As open-source releases and with some caveats, this study can also be used to
compare the performance of different cloud providers. While our assessment can
be used to determine the best cloud provider for any workload, it is
important to highlight that, due to differences in the underlying hardware and
software, each cloud system has a distinct network performance. Therefore,
when comparing cloud providers, the benchmark should be tailored to the
workload-of-interest, and the results should be interpreted in the light of
the specific characteristics of the hardware and software used by each cloud
provider.
  Finally, our study highlights the importance of considering the network
when assessing cloud systems for HPC workloads. While this is also true for
on-premise systems, cloud providers promote the scalability of their network
capabilities whereas on-premise administrators know the network performance
will scale with the workload. In contrast, users who do not account for the
network may end up with disappointing performance or even failed jobs in the
cloud.

droplet in an aerosol. Prior to entering the droplet, many particulates change

process negation effectively, we present CONDAQA, the first English reading

negated statements in paragraphs. We collect paragraphs with diverse negation
cues, then have crowdworkers ask questions about the implications of the
negated statement in the passage. We also have workers make three kinds of
edits to the passage -- paraphrasing the negated statement, changing the scope
of the negation, and reversing the negation -- resulting in clusters of
question-answer pairs that are difficult for models to answer with spurious
shortcuts. CONDAQA features 14,182 question-answer pairs with over 200 unique
negation cues and is challenging for current state-of-the-art models. The best
performing model on CONDAQA (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) achieves only 42% on our
consistency metric, well below human performance which is 81%. We release our
dataset, along with fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot evaluations, to
facilitate the development of future NLP methods that work on negated language.

dataset in hand, we hope to stimulate development of such models.

quantum system: Annealing explores equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian with
slowly changing parameters and can be exploited as a tool for solving complex
optimization problems. In contrast, quenches are sudden changes of the
Hamiltonian, producing a non-equilibrium situation. Here, we investigate the
relation between the two cases. Specifically, we show that the minimum of the
annealing gap, which is an important bottleneck of quantum annealing
algorithms, can be revealed from a dynamical quench parameter which describes
the dynamical quantum state after the quench. Combined with statistical tools
including the training of a neural network, the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics can be exploited to reproduce the full functional behavior
of the annealing gap from the quench data. We can then use this knowledge to
reveal the dynamical quantum state that is responsible for the observed
values of the annealing gap. This knowledge can in turn be used to optimize
quantum annealing protocols. The observed relation between quench and annealing
dynamics suggests itself as a tool for monitoring and understanding quantum
fluctuations in a quantum system.

into the quantum state responsible for the observed values of the annealing
gap. This knowledge can be used to develop more efficient quantum annealing
algorithms. The approach can be implemented in experimental settings to
investigate the obtained knowledge. In addition, our method can be expanded
to calculate other relevant quantities, e.g. the fidelities between the
microstate of the system and the target state. This will help to understand
the errors in a quantum annealing protocol and how they are connected to the
quench dynamics.

investigate the dynamical quantum state responsible for the observed values of
the annealing gap. This will help to understand the relation between quench and
annealing dynamics and how it is connected to the underlying many-body quantum

quantum annealing, our approach can be applied to other non-stationary

observed process behavior recorded in event data. Alignments are a
state-of-the-art technique to detect, localize, and quantify deviations in
process executions, i.e., traces, compared to reference process models.
Alignments, however, assume complete process executions covering the entire
process from start to finish or prefixes of process executions. This paper
defines infix/postfix alignments, proposes approaches to their computation, and
evaluates them using real-life event data.
  Given a trace and a process model, an infix/postfix alignment identifies a
segment as the part of the trace that significantly deviates from the process
model, and provides the exact boundaries of this segment, i.e., the prefix and
suffix parts not belonging to the infix/postfix deviation segment. We propose two
approaches to compute infix/postfix alignments, one based on frequency ratio and
another based on logistic regression. We evaluate these approaches using real-life
event data and process models. Our approach using frequency ratio is simple and
efficient. The approach using logistic regression provides more accurate results
and is suitable when different types of process model activities may have
different levels of adherence to the actual process behavior. Our evaluations
show that both approaches are effective in detecting process deviations and can
be used in conformance checking.

one-band physics and a Kondo-lattice--like regime emerge from the same

the system functions based on the changes of the software system. We implemented

reasonable accuracy and also has a good speedup.

species of BECs, which interact in different ways with an optical lattice, the

models discussed below reveal that the external acceleration of solitons is

asymmetric interaction between the two-component solitons, which can be

notably in cometary atmospheres and tails where sunlight produces exceptionally
bright near-UV to visible transitions. Such cations typically have
longer-wavelength and brighter electronic emission than their corresponding
neutrals. A robust understanding of their near-UV to visible properties would
allow these cations to be used as tools for probing the local plasma
environments or as tracers of neutral gas in cometary environments. However,
full spectral models are not possible for characterization of small, oxygen
containing cations given the body of molecular data currently available. To
fill this gap, we present ro-vibrational energy levels and transitions for the
$\mathrm{H_2O^+}$ cation up to about 0.6 cm$^{-1}$ energy separation, which
encompasses the typical temperatures found in cometary environments. This data
has been obtained by combining results from experimental techniques (FTIR and
Raman) with theoretical methods (variational methods and non-degenerate
perturbation theory). The resulting data set consists of 3441 fitted
transition energies, and covers 81 different transitions, with strengths
ranging from very faint ( $<10^{-6}$ W m$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$) to bright
($\approx10^{-3}$ W m$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$). The water cation transition
characteristics have been verified to be properly suited for illuminating
gaps in high-resolution spectra taken at spatial locations within or very
near the coma. Such spectra would greatly improve our understanding of
cometary physics and will motivate future detailed spectral modeling of
$\mathrm{H_2O^+}$ and its associated companions.

comets, the tail near-UV to visible brightness may provide a rough estimate of
the coma $\mathrm{H_2O^+$} abundance. Future in-coma spectral studies will
allow these quantities to be connected to physical processes in comets and will
assist in advancing cometary research towards understanding how comets form

as a sum of squares has a
long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some
specific rings (like integers or polynomials over the rationals), there are
known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for
many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of an
arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.
  From a computational number theory point of view, our algorithm is
implementable and efficient. We hope it to serve as a starting point for
developing more practical algorithms, and to provide examples and insights for
the ongoing automated proof verification projects, like the one by H. Cofman and
J. Cai, which tries to prove a version of the weak form of Hilbert's
irreducibility theorem, which asserts that there exists an element of $\Q[x]$
which is totally positive and irreducible.

new approach to traditional
spectroscopy where the spectral cross-correlation with a template spectrum can
be done entirely on-device. By creating photonic devices with a carefully
designed, modulated transmission spectrum, the cross-correlation can be carried
out optically without requiring any dispersion, vastly simplifying the
instrument and reducing its cost. The measured correlation lag can be used for
detecting atomic/molecular species within and determining the radial velocity
of a particular astrophysical object.
  We present an overview of two design approaches that are currently being
developed that use different photonic platforms: silicon and fibre-based
photonics. The silicon photonic approach utilizes ring resonators that can be
thermo-optically modulated to carry out the cross-correlation. The fibre
approach uses customized fibre Bragg gratings (FBGs) with transmission spectra
that can be strain-modulated. Both approaches have been able to detect
molecular gas in a lab setting, and we are now in the process of on-sky
testing.
  Lastly, we discuss the future for these types of devices as their simplicity
opens up the possibility of developing low-cost, purpose-built multi-object or
integral field spectroscopic instruments that could make significant
contributions to scientific programs requiring stellar RV measurements and
exoplanet detections.

polypharmacy side effect identification, drug-drug interaction prediction and
combination therapy design tasks have been proposed. Here, we present a unified
theoretical view of relational machine learning models which can address these
tasks. We provide fundamental definitions, compare existing model architectures
and discuss performance metrics, datasets and evaluation protocols. In
addition, we emphasize the importance of data augmentation and negative sampling
techniques. We go on to identify potential applications, limitations and
challenges in this domain of research. Finally, we point interested readers to
relevant datasets, software frameworks and relevant previous work. Through this
work, we aim to stimulate further research in this domain with the ultimate
goal of developing systems which can guide medical decision making with
high-accuracy.
  We demonstrate that existing models can be viewed through a lens of changing
data representation, choice of optimizer and architecture variation. We advocate
the use of positive sampling techniques for training relational models on
small-scale datasets. However, large-scale datasets may benefit from
aggressive data augmentation and sophisticated overloading schemes.
  We present a novel evaluation protocol which includes a performance metric
which incentivizes models to be conservative in their predictions. Models are
assigned a life-or-death label based on their performance on a small set of
critical DDIs. We show that current models fall short on the task of predicting
interactions for all possible drug pairs. Thus, there remains need for methods
which can learn more general representations of DDIs.
  Finally, we argue that the field will benefit from the use of control
experiments. These allow for evaluation of models on data generated under
different conditions. This could be used to gain insight into the working
mechanisms of models as well as to generally improve performance on unseen data.

model that fits data distributed on the nodes of a graph. We focus on Federated
Learning (FL) as a canonical application. One of the main challenges of FL is
the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has proven to delay convergence and bias
the model. In this work, we study random walk (RW) learning algorithms for
tackling the communication and data heterogeneity problems. The main idea is to
leverage available data to construct a model without ever collecting the data
on the PS. In a random walk, the nodes act as if they had all the data,
computing updates that depend on their own data and on the previous iterations
of the walk. This is possible if we allow persistent (repeated) deployments of
their local data and persistent state across several walks. While this is
practically infeasible, we show that a small number of persistent walks is
sufficient to achieve good model fitness. To our knowledge, this is the first
RW algorithm for FL with persistent state. Our analysis shows that our algorithm
achieves a sublinear convergence rate in the number of persistent walks, as
well as a low bias that can be made decrease exponentially with the number of
persistent walks. Simulation results on both synthetic and real datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm.

this condition satisfied for? To answer this question, we derive a condition on
the connectivity of the graph that is function of the heterogeneity of the data
and the desired bias level. Interestingly, this condition shows that the answer
depends on the strength of the communication bottleneck, as measured by the
length of the walks required by the algorithm. In particular, our analysis
reveals that homogeneous data or large heterogeneity together with sufficiently
long walks are sufficient to achieve low bias without needing persistent state on
more than a constant number of nodes. On the other hand, homogeneous data or

likelihood that offenders return to the criminal justice system in the future.

image segmentation tasks. In this paper, we introduce a novel regularization
strategy involving interpolation-based mixing for semi-supervised medical image
segmentation. The proposed method is a new consistency regularization strategy
that encourages segmentation of interpolation of two unlabelled data to be
consistent with the interpolation of segmentation maps. This is achieved by
interpolating the data and the segmentation maps in a way that the contribution
of individual data is inversely proportional to its distance to the nearest
available label. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in
combination with graph-based and adversarial loss functions for brain and colon
segmentation. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves
superior results compared to existing semi-supervised models while requiring
very few annotations.

in Deferred
Neural Rendering (DNR) provides a compelling balance between computational
complexity and realism of the resulting images. Using skinned meshes for
rendering articulating objects is a natural extension for the DNR framework and
would open it up to a plethora of applications. However, in this case the
neural shading step must account for deformations that are possibly not
captured in the mesh, as well as alignment inaccuracies and dynamics -- which
can confound the DNR pipeline. We present Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a
novel framework based on DNR which explicitly addresses its limitations for
virtual human avatars. We show the superiority of ANR not only with respect to
DNR but also with methods specialized for avatar creation and animation. In two
user studies, we observe a clear preference for our avatar model and we
demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on quantitative evaluation metrics.
Perceptually, we observe better temporal stability, level of detail and
plausibility.
  From a technical perspective, our model exploits the difference between
static anatomical alignment and dynamic skin alignment. We do so by learning a
mapping from the product of two alignments, one for the avatar anatomy and one
for the skin, to camera rays. We employ two rendering networks: a
\emph{static} network for the anatomical alignment, as in DNR, and a
\emph{dynamic} network, which takes the skin alignment as input. The image
produced by ANR is the combination of the two rendering networks, selectively
weighted by distance to the avatar's center. Through experiments, we show that
by allowing the dynamic network to capture possible alignment errors we can
improve the visual quality without increasing complexity.
  We also show that by splitting the viewing frustum into layers we can
efficiently produce detailed avatars for far-away segments of the skin. We
believe that ANR is a promising starting point for future developments in
virtual rendering and animation.

to infer on suicide excess deaths after a national emergency, authorities may
provide a rounded average of deaths before and after the emergency started.
Suicide rates tend to be relatively low around the world and such rounding may
seriously affect inference on the change of suicide rate. In this paper, we
study the scenario when a rounded to nearest integer average is used to
estimate a non-negative discrete random variable. Specifically, our interest is
in drawing inference on a parameter from the pmf of Y, when we get U = n[Y/n]
as a proxy for Y. The probability generating function of U, E(U), and Var(U)
capture the effect of the coarsening of the support of Y. Also, moments and
estimators of distribution parameters are explored for some special cases. We
show that under certain conditions, there is little impact from rounding.
However, we also find scenarios where rounding can significantly affect
statistical inference as demonstrated in two applications. The simple methods
we propose are able to partially counter rounding error effects.

well as estimating overdose deaths and fatalities from drinking and driving.
We find that the rounded average before and after the emergency start can
seriously affect the inference on change of suicide rate, but using U for
estimating total suicide deaths in a particular time period is relatively
stable.
  To estimate the number of deaths due to overdose under counting bias, we find
that rounding of quarterly averages can significantly impact the estimate, but
rounding of annual averages has little impact.
  To estimate fatalities from drinking and driving, we find that rounding of
monthly averages can seriously affect the estimate, but running average can
partially mitigate the effect.

hexagonal rare-earth indium oxides GdInO$_3$ have been studied by combing
experiments and model calculations. The two inequivalent Gd$^{3+}$ ions form
the centered honeycomb lattice, which consists of honeycomb and triangular
sublattices. The dc magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements
suggest two antiferromagnetic phase transitions at $T_\textrm{N1}$ = 2.3 K and
$T_\textrm{N2}$ = 1.02 K. An inflection point is observed in the isothermal
magnetization curve, which implies an up-up-down phase with a 1/3 magnetization
plateau. We also observe a large magnetic entropy change originated from the
magnetic frustration in GdInO$_3$. By considering a classical spin Hamiltonian,
we establish the ground state phase diagram, which suggests that GdInO$_3$ has
a weak easy-axis anisotropy and is close to the equilateral triangular-lattice
system. The theoretical ground-state phase diagram may be used as a reference
in NMR, ESR, or $\mu$SR experiments in future.
  In conclusion, GdInO$_3$ is a candidate of weak easy-axis spin ice material
with plateaued magnetization. The magnetic entropy change original from the
frustrated honeycomb lattice should be useful in searching other magnetic
phases in various honeycomb lattice materials.

  As UDA datasets often suffer from a lack of sufficient target annotations,
prevalent pseudo-labeling methods \cite{Temirbekov2022} rely on accurate
over-segmentation of the target images. Unfortunately, such methods are
sensitive to occasional errors in the pseudo-labels, e.g.\ misclassified
background pixels. In this work, we propose to use multi-observer pseudo-labels
instead of single-image based approaches. We train a network on the source
domain and use its predictions on the target images. To obtain the pseudo-label
at a particular location, we 'translate' the prediction map from the source to
the target in a way that allows for segmentation errors in the target images
and also enables appearance variability due to different illumination conditions
and segmentation errors. With our segmentation-aware image translations, we
generate multiple pseudo-labels for each target image by varying the
segmentation mask used for the projection. We show on two benchmark datasets,

abundant and relatively easy to obtain, it is unclear how to leverage these

unsupervised and domain adaptation ReID methods utilize only the public
datasets in their experiments, with labels removed. In addition, due to small
data sizes, these methods usually rely on fine tuning by the unlabeled training

progress of large-scale self-supervised image classification using contrastive
learning, we propose to learn ReID representation from large-scale unlabeled
surveillance video alone. Assisted by off-the-shelf pedestrian detection tools,
we apply the contrastive loss at both the image and the tracklet levels.
Together with a principal component analysis step using camera labels freely
available, our evaluation using a large-scale unlabeled dataset shows far
superior performance among unsupervised methods that do not use any training
data in the testing domain. Furthermore, the accuracy improves with the data
size and therefore our method has great potential with even larger and more
diversified datasets.

models on three camera view classification datasets. Our models have a clear
preference for medium to high camera views and perform the best on the downtown
dataset.

best among all unsupervised methods that do not use any training data in the
testing domain, while the existing methods specialize in the city-level.
Again, the accuracy improves with the data size and therefore our method has a
great potential with even larger and more diverse datasets.

from the following sources: Baidu Road Dataset, U-Garment Dataset, Street

practical utility in real world surveillance scenarios.

circuit depth. In this study, the toric code is used as a benchmark to compare
the performance of two-qubit and five-qubit gates within parity-check circuits.
We consider trapped ion qubits that are controlled via Raman transitions, where
the primary source of error is assumed to be spontaneous photon scattering. We
show that a five-qubit M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate offers an approximately
$40\%$ improvement over two-qubit gates in terms of the fault tolerance
threshold. This result indicates an advantage of using multi-qubit gates in the
context of QEC.

toric code concatenated with another toric code (a "tangled" code). The
gains achieved by the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate for this particular circuit

multi-qubit gates with QEC when the code distance that is needed to achieve a
desired error rate is not small.

implemented with high fidelity relative to its gate time, it may be preferable
to use it instead of several two-qubit gates. If the fidelity of the gate is
too low, it may be necessary to use an ancilla-based method to implement a
effective five-qubit gate, which is likely to be the better option in this case
as well.

relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By

the KQI, the greater the system disorder, and the greater the knowledge amount

evolution of knowledge growth in the system, that is, the faster the growth
curve, the greater the knowledge generation capacity of the system, and the

is a type of powerful deep neural network that
has been widely used in many sequence analysis and modeling applications.
However, the large model size problem of LSTM networks make their practical
deployment still very challenging, especially for the video recognition tasks
that require high-dimensional input data. Aiming to overcome this limitation
and fully unlock the potentials of LSTM models, in this paper we propose to
perform algorithm and hardware co-design towards high-performance
energy-efficient LSTM networks. At algorithm level, we propose to develop fully
decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure-based LSTM, namely FDHT-LSTM,
which enjoys ultra-low model complexity while still achieving high accuracy. In
order to fully reap such attractive algorithmic benefit, we further develop the
corresponding customized hardware architecture to support the efficient
execution of the proposed FDHT-LSTM model. With the delicate design of memory
access scheme, the complicated matrix transformation can be efficiently
supported by the underlying hardware without any access conflict in an
on-the-fly way. Our evaluation results show that both the proposed
ultra-compact FDHT-LSTM models and the corresponding hardware accelerator
achieve very high performance. Compared with the state-of-the-art compressed
LSTM models, FDHT-LSTM enjoys both order-of-magnitude reduction in model size
and significant accuracy improvement across different video recognition
datasets. Meanwhile, compared with the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed
model-oriented hardware designs, our proposed HDH supports not only the
efficient execution of FDHT-LSTMs but also a very high reusability for other
tensor decomposed models.
  We believe that the attractive performance achieved by the proposed
ultra-compact FDHT-LSTM models and the corresponding hardware accelerator
makes it a very promising candidate for video recognition applications and other
sequence analysis domains where high-performance, efficient, and scalable
LSTM-based solutions are in high demand.
  In this open-source paper, we provide not only the algorithmic designs of the
proposed FDHT-LSTM models but also the corresponding hardware architecture
development. Our contributions provide a clean separation of algorithm and
hardware design, and are generally applicable to other sequence analysis
domains. They make the promising FDHT-LSTM approach more accessible to a
wider range of practitioners and researchers.
  We believe that our work makes meaningful contributions to the field of
deep-learning-based video recognition, and provides an interesting case study of
how to achieve high performance via delicate algorithm and hardware design
together.

cognitive sciences. Bayes
factors provide one general way to compare different hypotheses by their
compatibility with the observed data. Those quantifications can then also be
used to choose between hypotheses. While Bayes factors provide an immediate
approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a tool for Bayesian inferences and
discuss that utility functions are needed for principled decisions on
hypotheses. Next, we study how Bayes factors misbehave under different
conditions. This includes a study of errors in the estimation of Bayes factors.
Importantly, it is unknown whether Bayes factor estimates based on bridge
sampling are unbiased for complex analyses. We are the first to use
simulation-based calibration as a tool to test the accuracy of Bayes factor
estimates. Moreover, we study how stable Bayes factors are against different
MCMC draws. We moreover study how Bayes factors depend on variation in the
data. We also look at variability of decisions based on Bayes factors and how
to optimize decisions using a utility function. We outline a Bayes factor
analysis protocol that includes how to decide on the number of different
samples to use for the Bayes factor estimation. Furthermore, we present a
software toolkit for easy implementation of Bayes factor analyses. And we
provide a detailed guideline on how to perform Bayes factor analyses from
theorem to practice. In conclusion, Bayes factor analyses can be carried out
with high reliability by following our protocol. However, Bayes factor
estimates may be imprecise if a large number of samples is used. We outline
how to optimize decisions using a utility function and obtain essentially
perfect results in terms of correctness of decisions. Moreover, Bayes factors
are unstable against different MCMC samples. We suggest using the premium of
decisions by using a moderate number of samples (around 10^5) and a careful
protocol to minimize variability of decisions. Finally, we recommend to couple
Bayes factor analyses with utility functions to ensure that the simplest
hypothesis is tried first and that all hypotheses with a reasonable
probability are explicitly considered.

employing a B-spline basis in a finite-size box. Convergence of the
self-consistency iterations for the occupied electron orbitals is achieved by

sembles of coupled oscillators map
to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, explosive synchronization transitions, which
facilitate fast, abrupt changes between these functional states, has recently
seen significant interest from researchers. While previous work has identified
properties of complex systems that support explosive synchronization, these
investigations have been conducted largely on an ad-hoc basis. Here we provide
an exact criterion for explosive synchronization in coupled phase oscillator
ensembles by investigating the necessary relationship between dynamical and
structural disorder. This result provides a critical step towards untangling
the intertwined properties of complex systems responsible for abrupt phase
transitions and bistability in biological and engineered systems.
Furthermore, we find that this criterion can be used to optimize network
design to generate explosive synchronization in a desired range of system
sizes. Our work may also provide new insights into the role of abrupt phase
transitions in the failure of complex systems.
Finally, we show that the exact solution can be used to investigate various
phenomena in biological and engineered systems, including the synchronization
of insect swarms and the stability of power grids.
Specifically, we find that explosive synchronization is crucial for the
maintenance of swarm cohesion in large insect ensembles and may play a central
role in the loss of stability in modern power grids.
In both cases, cooperative behavior at the edge of a critical transition may
lead to a disaster.
Therefore, understanding the role of explosive synchronization in these
systems is vital for improving their performance and preventing catastrophic
failure.
Overall, our work provides a fundamental framework for investigating
synchronization in complex systems and has relevant applications to studying
and designing the active states of biological and engineered systems.
Finally, we make our numerical code available open-source to facilitate
investigations of related phenomena.
As such, this work may provide new insights into the design of active systems
with robust, abrupt switching behavior and may help to understand the loss of
stability in modern power grids.

infected individuals during coughing, sneezing, speaking and breathing. The
spread of the infection and hence its menace depend on how the virus-loaded
droplets evolve in space and time with changing environmental conditions. In
view of this, we investigate the evolution of the droplets within the purview
of the Brownian motion of the evaporating droplets in the air with varying
weather conditions under the action of gravity. We track the movement of the
droplets till either they gravitationally settle on the ground or evaporate to
aerosols of size 2$\mu$m or less. Droplets with radii $2 \mu$m or less may
continue to diffuse and remain suspended in the air for long time. The effects
of relative humidity and temperature on the evaporation are found to be
significant. We note that under strong flowing conditions droplets travel large
distances. It is found that the bigger droplets fall on the ground due to the
dominance of gravity over the diffusive force despite the loss of mass due to
evaporation. The smaller evaporating droplets may not settle on the ground but
remain suspended in the air due to the dominance of the diffusive force. The
fate of the intermediate size droplets depends on the weather conditions and
play crucial roles in the spread of the infection. These environment dependent
effects may be included in a model to study the spread of the infection.
Moreover, such studies may also be applicable to other infectious diseases.
  From the point of view of a statistical physics problem, we explain the
formation of the COVID19 pandemic through the occupation of states representing
different levels of infections. The occupation of different states is governed
by a Fokker-Planck equation obtained under assuming the presence of a large
number of infected individuals in a population. The solution to the equation
shows exponential distribution for the number of days an individual remains
infectious. The average duration of being infectious is found to be $2$ days.
Moreover, more than $50\%$ population remain infectious for $1$ day or less. A
discussion on the usefulness of such a statistical analysis is presented.
Further, we propose a simple model involving three states to understand the
spread of the infection through droplets and the efficacy of washing of hands,
use of mask and social distancing. The model reveals the importance of all
these activities in containing the pandemic.

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there
is also uncertainty due to limited data, but also due to NN hyperparameters,
overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in NNs, there is no systematic investigation of suitable
methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently
even for function approximation, and there is even less work on solving partial
differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
on prototype problems, including problems with mixed input-output data, and
stochastic problems in high dimensions. In the Appendix, we include a
comprehensive description of all the UQ methods employed, which we will make
available as a Python package. Our results show that some methods work
surprisingly well even in challenging settings, while others fail. To help
design better NN UQ protocols, we present guidelines on how to evaluate
performance of UQ methods, which includes reporting training and test data,
metric curves, and uncertainty maps. To demonstrate the value of our framework
we present two applications, namely on data-scarce problems with
heterogeneous data and on a problem involving extreme events. Overall, our
work lays the foundation towards developing a new generation of robust and

integrals with eigenvalues of the commutator operators. We show through

entropy in both $N\to \infty$ and $g\to 0$ limits. Moreover, we extend the
unitary matrix model to the multi-plaquette model, and find that the
expectation value of the product of unitary matrices is proportional to the
product of Euler angles.

) have become an established part of
numerous safety-critical computer vision applications, including human robot
interactions and automated driving. Real-world implementations will need to
guarantee their robustness against hardware soft errors corrupting the
underlying platform memory. Based on the previously observed efficacy of
activation clipping techniques, we build a prototypical safety case for
classifier CNNs by demonstrating that range supervision represents a highly
reliable fault detector and mitigator with respect to relevant bit flips,
adopting an eight-exponent floating point data representation. We further
explore novel, non-uniform range restriction methods that effectively suppress
the probability of silent data corruptions. As a next step, researchers and
developers can utilize the evidence presented in this work to argue for the
use of existing defense techniques that can repair errors caused by hardware
soft errors, thus enabling the deployment of safety-critical AI applications.
We make our evidence available in an accompanying repository.
  Which activation range restriction is best suited for a particular safety-critical
AI application? To answer this question, we introduce AGarage, a novel, modular
safety certification framework for CNNs that quickly explores a vast design
space encompassing various activation range restrictions, while maintaining a
tight connection to the underlying proof. With AGarage, researchers and
developers can easily prototype and test new range designs by adjusting a few
parameters, thereby significantly accelerating the path towards proof-based
design. We demonstrate that a carefully designed activation range restriction
achieves a higher reliability than other hardening techniques currently in use.
We make our framework available in an accompanying repository.
  Researchers have developed various techniques to evaluate the performance of
proof-based safety certifications. We present DaliCorp, a novel, mutually
exclusive dataset of certified CNNs that allows researchers to train, evaluate,
and compare new evidence generation techniques. With DaliCorp, researchers can
also study various evidence-dependent characteristics of modern CNNs, and thus
further refine evidence generation techniques to match the evidence needs of
real-world applications. We make our dataset available in an accompanying
repository.

  Critical computer vision applications will need to run evidence-based
classifiers, which will be checked for defects at runtime to ensure continued
correctness. To this end, we present a proof-of-concept framework that enables
the efficient measurement of evidence on GPU-accelerated classifiers. With this
framework, researchers can easily prototype and test evidence-related techniques
by leveraging our evidence utilities and measurement routines.

tracking (DST). However, substantial noise has been discovered in its state
annotations. Such noise brings about huge challenges for training DST models
robustly. Although several refined versions, including MultiWOZ 2.1-2.4, have
been published recently, there are still lots of noisy labels, especially in
the training set. Besides, it is costly to rectify all the problematic
annotations. In this paper, instead of improving the annotation quality
further, we propose a general framework, named ASSIST (lAbel noiSe-robuSt
dIalogue State Tracking), to train DST models robustly from noisy labels.
ASSIST first generates pseudo labels for each sample in the training set by
using an auxiliary model trained on a small clean dataset, then puts the
generated pseudo labels and vanilla noisy labels together to train the primary
model. We show the validity of ASSIST theoretically. Experimental results also
demonstrate that ASSIST improves the joint goal accuracy of DST by up to

non-local model that successfully described the French riots of 2005 to
incorporate the topology of Santiago's subway network and explain the reported
distribution of rioting activity in the city. Although the model reproduced the

displacement mechanism can be studied using tools from graph theory,

due to the complexity of the resulting model, an analysis of its behavior is
challenging to carry out. Consequently, this report focuses on assembling the
