Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., on overcast days
and water-filled ground, which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to
extract visual features. Experiments validate that it outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.
  We observe from strong ray tracing experiments that most of the estimation
error indeed comes from back light and shadow, which are difficult features for
traditional computer vision algorithms to extract. Therefore, our solution is
particularly suitable for the scenes which are commonly seen in daily life, such
as under strong sunlight and on transparent ground (e.g. ice, water, etc.).
Besides, our model has a potential application on extraterrestrial planetary
landing, where the ground are usually on transparent ice. It could provide a
robust and accurate pose estimation for the landing craft, which is crucial
for successful landing.

  The study of parafermion vertex operator algebra associated to integrable highest
weight module for simple affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ was started by
Dunkl in 2010. In 2013, he found a vertex operator algebra (VOA) structure on the
module $V^{(r)}$ with $r$ being an admissible integer of $[s] = \frac{1}{s+1}$,
$0<s<n$. Although we have some equivalent conditions for admissible integers,
the range of values for admissible $r$ remains unknown so far. It is unknown
whether there exist admissible $r$ other than those in the form $[s]$, or
whether there are other simple highest weight modules for $osp(1|2n)$. These
unknowns make it very difficult to completely understand the structure of
multi-layer parafermion VOAs associated to $osp(1|2n)$. In this paper, assuming
$r=[s]$ and collecting relevant equalities, we succeed in determining the
generators for the parafermion VOA associated to $V^{(r)}$ with $r=[s]$.
particularly, we confirm that the set of generators does not depend on the
specific value of $s$, as long as $s$ belongs to the set of admissible integers.
This further justifies the notations of $V^{(r)}$ and the superalgebra
$osp(1|2n)$ when $r=[s]$. It would be interesting to study the same problem
for $EXT^{(r)}(V^{(s)}, l)$ and the general boson-steroid superalgebra.
Unfortunately, the current formalism is not suitable for such generalizations.
We hope our formalism can be extended to study the representation theory of
simple 2-parameter  Lie superalgebras.

knowledge-amalgamation problem, termed
Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA). The goal of FedSA is to train a
student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and non-identically distributed.
To make things more challenging, (1) each teacher has only one sample per class;
(2) all the data are re-indexed with different labels in the student domain;
(3) there is a non-trivial feature domain shift between teachers and students;
and (4) the participating teachers are "passive", i.e., they do not want to
collect any new data nor perform any extra computation. To tackle the difficulty
(4), we propose a novel strategy called $K$-HashSA, which assumes the teachers
and the students are all equipped with a similar hashing capability. More
specifically, each teacher will generate a pseudo-data called
"co-training sample" that can be shared with other teachers and/or the student;
and all the data as well as the co-training samples are indexed with hash
functions. Via exchanging the co-training samples, even with only one sample per
class, the teachers can provide more knowledge to the student. Extensive
experiments on six benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed
FedSA knowledge-amalgamation framework and the superiority of the
K-HashSA approach over strong baselines.

evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the volatile sources and sinks.
Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including
the role of Late Accretion impacts, how magnetic field generation is tied into
long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical
feedback cycles for atmospheric evolution. We highlight plausible end-member
evolutionary pathways that Venus could have followed, from accretion to its
present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the
planet was desiccated by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase. In a

MacPherson gave a local and combinatorial formula for the
Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We give an expanded version of
their discussion and highlight the origins of combinatorial differential
manifolds in their work.
  Gelfand & MacPherson (1992) attach to each combinatorial differential
manifold $M$ a chain complex whose Pontrjagin classes are the cup product
multiplication of the classes attached to the vertices of $M$. We show that this
construction is precisely the sheaf-theoretic operation of cup product passed
to the quotient by isomorphism, recovering combinatorially the well-known
connection between differential manifolds and simplicial complexes equipped with
differential forms.
  We also discuss the connection between the combinatorial differential
manifolds of Gelfand & MacPherson (1992) and the more recent theory of
singular spaces. It is well known that the theory of singular spaces provides a
natural generalization of differential manifolds to a larger class of geometric
spaces in which the Pontrjagin classes can be defined. It follows from
Thom's work that any combinatorial differential manifold $M$ corresponds to a
singular space, but in our formulation, $M$ itself is enough to compute its
Pontrjagin classes.
  Finally, we sketch how the formula can be generalized to other cohomology
theories such as Chern--Simons classes.
  Gelfand & MacPherson (1992) give a straightforward algorithm for computing the
Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold $M$. We demonstrate the algorithm
on three increasing levels of sophistication: (1) We define combinatorial
differential manifolds and show how to compute their Pontrjagin classes using
their chain complexes. (2) We introduce a simple graphical language - handle
decompositions - which is more intuitive than the quasioriented simple graphs of
combinatorial differential manifolds. We define a natural functor between the
two categories and show how to compute Pontrjagin classes using handle
decompositions. (3) We consider the differential manifolds represented by
CW-complexes. We define a natural way to construct CW-complexes from handle
decompositions and show how to compute the Pontrjagin classes using either
method.

for visually rich
documents like invoices is the cost of acquiring the several thousand
high-quality labeled documents that are needed to train a model with acceptable
accuracy. We propose Selective Labeling to simplify the labeling task to
provide "yes/no" labels for candidate extractions predicted by a model trained
on partially labeled documents. We combine this with a custom active learning
strategy to find the predictions that the model is most uncertain about. We
show through experiments on document types drawn from 3 different domains that
selective labeling can reduce the cost of acquiring labeled data by $10\times$
with a negligible loss in accuracy.
  We also observe that the model learns to rely on easy predictions (e.g.,
plain text that clearly matches a extraction format) early on in training and
leaves uncertainty about more complex extractions (e.g., text with misspelled
words that match a extraction format). We propose the Latent Space Filter to
remove these easy predictions before feeding the rest of the data to a model.
We show that the latent space filter helps to increase the model's accuracy on
unlabeled data by $3\times$.
  Finally, we observe that the distribution of extractions can be very different
across many documents in a dataset (e.g., terms that are commonly paid late vs
early). We propose the Layered Dataset Organizers to group extractions by
category and track the distribution of extractions that are typically present in
each group. We show that the layered organizers can be trained to predict the
likely extractions present in a document based on visual features, to locate
them to the right place in the document, and to provide a protocol for evaluating
extraction models on a very natural level of granularity (per category vs
per-document).

Interferometer Collaborations have now detected all three classes of compact
binary mergers: binary black hole (BBH), binary neutron star (BNS), and neutron
star-black hole (NSBH). For coalescences involving neutron stars, the
simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation
produced by an event, has broader potential to enhance our understanding of
these events, and also to probe the equation of state (EOS) of dense matter.
However, electromagnetic follow-up to gravitational wave (GW) events requires
rapid real-time detection and classification of GW signals, and conventional
detection approaches are computationally prohibitive for the anticipated rate
of detection of next-generation GW detectors. In this work, we present the
first deep learning based results of classification of GW signals from NSBH
mergers in \textit{real} LIGO data. We show for the first time that a deep
neural network can successfully distinguish all three classes of compact binary
mergers and separate them from detector noise. Specifically, we train a
convolutional neural network (CNN) on $\sim 500,000$ data samples of real LIGO
noise with injected BBH, BNS, and NSBH GW signals, and we show that our network
has high sensitivity and accuracy. Most importantly, we successfully recover
the two confirmed NSBH merger events, NS merger event candidate GW190425, and
generate classification probability distributions for $\sim 27$ months of
real LIGO data taken during the first and second LIGO observing runs (O1 and
O2). Our results confirm that deep learning methods can provide high quality
classification of all three classes of compact binary mergers and can be used
as a preliminary online analysis in the presence of real detector noise.
Furthermore, our results can also be used to aid the development of more
advanced GW detection pipelines.

development and refinement of deep learning based GW detection pipelines.
Finally, we provide all the necessary data and hyperparameters used in this
work, to ensure reproducibility of results.

urban
environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity in the early
stages of the pandemic, behavioral changes including lower willingness to
explore new places and changes in visitation preferences further worsened the
long-term diversity of encounters. Our findings suggest that the pandemic could
have long-lasting negative effects on urban income diversity, and provide
implications for managing the trade-off between the stringency of COVID-19
policies and the diversity of urban encounters as we move beyond the pandemic.
  Overall, our approach illustrates how to leverage mobility data to study
urban social interactions and their changes over time, and how such studies can
contribute new insights to address broader societal questions.
  We make the following contributions available to promote further research:
- A high-quality, anonymized mobility dataset of over one million users
encompassing four US cities collected across three years; - A set of
methodologies developed in this work for analyzing urban social interactions and
their changes over time; and - The code used in this work (available at
https://github.com/haozhezhang/UrbanEncounterDiversity) that incorporates a
variety of established analytical tools.
  As mobility data continues to be collected in various forms and scales, we
believe that such data and methodologies have the potential to be applied to
the investigation of a wide variety of questions, including but not limited to
the impact of other global events on urban diversity, the effect of different
policies on urban income diversity, and the relationship between urban
diversity and economic productivity.

a complex task
for autonomous mobile platforms. Especially when conditions worsen, typical
sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally. In this study, we investigate
the performance of a navigation system operating in a dynamic indoor environment
with a mobile platform equipped with a lidar, a high-definition camera, and an
IMU. We experiment with various scenes and conditions while monitoring system
performance. Our findings show that with present sensor technology, the system
can operate reliably in medium rain conditions and smoke, but may fail when
large amounts of water are present or in very dusty conditions. Furthermore,
the system can navigate through moving people, but may recover poorly after
being bumped. We also find that the system can operate under low-light conditions
but may fail when light is absent. Finally, we observe that the system can
navigate through curved obstacles, but with poorer performance than straight
obstacles. Based on our findings, we discuss areas for future improvement.
  We make two major contributions. First, we provide a framework for systematically

fields and the shape operator. In particular, we show that the total mean
curvature corresponds to the sum of the shape operator's eigenvalues. We
examine cases leading to non-negative, non-positive, and mixed total mean
curvatures.

values of the shape operator in Gaussian random fields. We address questions
such as the likelihood of non-negative, non-positive, or mixed eigenvalues and
quantify the range of eigenvalues. Moreover, we analyze the distribution of the
standard deviations of eigenvalues and their products with the number of points
in the system. This leads to a better understanding of how surface curvature
varies in space.

optimizing their total mean curvature. We propose a dynamic framework based on
the Laplace-Beltrami operator that allows us to minimize or maximize the total
mean curvature on a given surface represented by a random field. We demonstrate
the effectiveness of this approach on various surfaces.

minimizing/maximizing the total mean curvature, we aim at creating surfaces
exhibiting specified levels of curvature. We demonstrate the utility of this
modification by creating surfaces with holes, handles, and wavy patterns.

manner, the surface of a fish swimming in water. We, thus, propose a novel

computer graphics and animation.

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) as a typical robust
alternative of the conventional PCA has enjoyed great popularity over the past
years. In this work, we consider a rotationally invariant L1-PCA, which is
hardly studied in the literature. To tackle it, we propose a proximal
alternating linearized minimization method with a nonlinear extrapolation for
solving its two-block reformulation. Moreover, we show that the proposed method
converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated
problem. Such a point is proved to be a critical point of the original problem
under a condition imposed on the step size. Finally, we conduct numerical
experiments on both synthetic and real datasets to support our theoretical
developments and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.
  As L1-PCA is an optimization problem, there exist various iterative methods
for solving it. One may wonder why we need to consider its rotational invariant
formulation. In fact, the rotational invariance is an implicitly assumed
property of the PCAs, and the rotational invariant L1-PCA reflects more closely
the conventional PCA. Moreover, its reformulation into a two-block problem
allows us to develop a simple and efficient algorithm for solving it. Most importantly, our theoretical analysis for the proposed algorithm also applies to the conventional L1-PCA, and thus we believe that our work is self-contained and has its own values.

polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.

such as a pulse with a large amplitude and a rotational hump. For the first time,
we detected a high-energy cutoff in the optical pulse of an asynchronous polar,
a feature that is common in synchrotron-emitting magnetic CVs. The cutoff in the
pulse profile indicates an energy at which the number of photons is reduced to
one tenth of the peak, which is about 0.035% of the binary's total energy out.
Furthermore, we detected a second, lower-amplitude pulse with a similar shape to
the primary pulse, which we attribute to a non-thermal, synchrotron emission
component caused by electrons accelerated in a second, possibly dipolar
magnetic field polarity. This is the first direct observational evidence for
multiple magnetic polarities in an asynchronous polar.

the solid problems all at once. We then present another reduction technique
that is based on a partitioned (or segregated) procedure: the fluid and the

test case, with a fluid Reynolds number Re = 100.

reduce the computational time needed to solve FSI problems, and to illustrate the
different behavior of the two reduction procedures, depending on the particular
test case considered. Further investigations are needed in order to assess the
efficacy of the RB methods with respect to the solution error and to the
computational time. At the moment, we can however say that the RB procedures
presented illustrate a very promising direction of research towards the
reduction of the computational time needed to solve complex FSI problems.

presented in [1, 2]. The two references contain all the technical details of

been an unsolved question of high-energy astrophysics. One approach for solving
this puzzle is to correlate UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, since neutrinos
are a direct probe of hadronic interactions of cosmic rays and are not
deflected by magnetic fields. In this paper, we present three different
approaches for correlating the arrival directions of neutrinos with the arrival
directions of UHECRs. The neutrino data is provided by the IceCube Neutrino
Observatory and ANTARES, while the UHECR data with energies above $\sim$50 EeV
is provided by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. All
experiments provide increased statistics and improved reconstructions with
respect to our previous results reported in 2015. The first analysis uses a
high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source searches to search
for excesses of neutrinos clustering in the vicinity of UHECR directions. The
second analysis searches for an excess of UHECRs in the direction of the
highest-energy neutrinos. The third analysis searches for an excess of pairs of
UHECRs and highest-energy neutrinos on different angular scales. None of the
analyses has found a significant excess, and previously reported
over-fluctuations are reduced in significance. Based on these results, we have
not found evidence for a correlation of UHECRs with neutrinos, but we have
increased our knowledge of the fluence limit in the case of a point-like
source. Considering the importance of continued sensitivity improvements and
potential systematic errors, we recommend that future UHECR and neutrino
experiments, in particular the Square Kilometre Array, include correlations as
a fundamental analysis topic.

nonequilibrium thermodynamics to study expansion/contraction processes. Here,
the numbers of initial and final microstates are different so they cannot be
connected by unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This commonly happens when the
phase space volume changes, and has not been studied so far using Hamiltonian
trajectories that can be inverted to yield an identity mapping between initial
and final microstates as the parameter in the Hamiltonian is changed. We
propose a trick to overcome this hurdle with a focus on free expansion in an
isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different
from the exchange microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes. We also establish
that the microwork is nonnegative for free expansion, which is remarkable,
since its sign is not fixed in a general process.
  We have developed a new statistical method to identify nonequilibrium
microstates. According to this method, a microstate is localized in a
nonequilibrium correlation pattern of particles, which is manifested in the
variation of the correlation function across the system. We have investigated
whether the microwork is nonzero at the boundary of the correlation pattern
during free expansion. It is found that the microwork is nonzero and can be
irreversibly large at the boundary, where the kinetic energy is mainly dissipated.
Defining the boundary is highly fluctuation-dependent. The permanently zero
micowork in the interior implies that the interior microparticles move
coherently, leading to the cancellation of the micowork. The coherent motion in
the interior may be triggered by the large kinetic energy deposited by the
moving macroparticles at the boundary. Our results provide insight into how
microstates expand internally and externally.
  We investigate the effect of an harmonic potential on the correlation pattern.
It is found that the harmonic potential mainly affects the boundary of the
correlation pattern, pushing its location deeper into the system, where the
potential is stronger. The internal correlation pattern, which is responsible for
the majority of the microwork, is almost unaffected by the harmonic potential.
This is because the characteristic frequency of the correlation is significantly
lower than that of the harmonic potential in all the situations considered.

through the various steps of GCNN operation and learning both visually and
numerically.

related NNs. It provides a unified account of GCNNs and its variants (e.g.,
graph auto-encoders, generative models) and helps in removing concepts that are
too abstract. It is ideally suited for practitioners (who are already
familiar with the basics of NNs) who want to leverage the power of GCNNs in
their applications. It can also be used as educational material for teaching
NNs and signal processing concepts (e.g., matched filtering, system
identification) in an undergraduate/graduate electrical engineering course.

and demonstrating how with some modifications a well-established NN class

the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.

but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To this end, in this work, we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting high-dose to low-dose by simply changing the AdaIN code. Thanks to
the shared baseline network, the additional memory requirement and weight
increases are minimized, and the training can be done more stably even with
small training data. Experimental results show that the proposed method

from training on multiple related tasks by exploiting similarities among them.
At the same time, the trained agent is able to solve a wider range of different
problems. While this effect is well documented for model-free multi-task
methods, we demonstrate a detrimental effect when using a single learned
dynamics model for multiple tasks. Thus, we address the fundamental question of
whether model-based multi-task reinforcement learning benefits from shared
dynamics models in a similar way model-free methods do from shared policy
networks. Using a single dynamics model, we see clear evidence of task
confusion and reduced performance. As such, our results question the benefits of
multi-task learning when using a model that predicts over the full state space.
As a remedy, we propose an intuitive state-bounded multi-task dynamics model,
that dramatically reduces the effect of task interference. The new model allows
for significant learning speedups --by approximately an order of magnitude --
while maintaining or increasing task performance.

useful extrapolation behavior, reducing the reliance on tight bounds that may
otherwise lead to suboptimal behavior. These findings are demonstrated across a
variety of cart-pole scenarios and a robotic navigation task.

applications. It is often the case that many image hypotheses are consistent
with both the measurements and prior information, and so the goal is not to
recover a single "best" hypothesis but rather to explore the space of probable
hypotheses, i.e., to sample from the posterior distribution. In this work, we
propose a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that can generate dozens of
high-quality posterior samples per second. Using quantitative evaluation
metrics like conditional Fr\'{e}chet inception distance, we demonstrate that
our method produces state-of-the-art posterior samples in both multicoil MRI
and inpainting applications.
  By using a conditional generator, we can produce detailed, natural-looking
samples in a matter of milliseconds. Additionally, we show that these samples
are not only visually indistinguishable but also have low conditional
statistical difference to separable solutions like CSIR and other upscaling
methods. We believe that by increasing the flexibility of the generator (at the
cost of some realism) one may be able to improve the quality of the samples.
This could be achieved by adding semantically meaningful noise, using more
complex modules (e.g. recurrent networks), or joint optimization with a
statistical prior.

the THz communication is conventionally envisioned for short-range wireless
applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication

training schemes, such as exhaustive search or hierarchical methods with a
fixed number of training levels, can lead to a very large time overhead. To
address this challenge, in this paper, a novel hierarchical beam training
scheme with dynamic training levels is proposed to optimize the performance of
multi-hop THz links. In fact, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize
the overall spectral efficiency of the multi-hop THz link by dynamically and
jointly selecting the number of beam training levels across all the constituent
single-hop links. To solve this problem in presence of unknown channel state
information, noise, and path loss, a new reinforcement learning solution based
on the multi-armed bandit (MAB) is developed. Simulation results show the fast
convergence of the proposed scheme in presence of random channels and noise.
The results also show that the proposed scheme can yield up to 75% performance
gain, in terms of spectral efficiency, compared to the conventional

scattering screens, most of
unknown origin. Scintillation studies of pulsars provides a sensitive tool for
resolving these scattering screens and a means of measuring their properties.
In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, with the highest-precision distance measurement placing a screen at
just $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from the Earth. We associate the more distant of
these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.
  We also report the appearance of a new scattering screen near the Earth,
previously undetected. The new screen was revealed by a previously-unknown
outburst of scattering, which is attributed to a cloud flowing from a known
source of high-energy particles, Cygnus X-2. The timescale for the event is
consistent with the timescale for interaction with the ISM, indicating that the
pulsar environment is not dominating the interaction. The density of the
cloud has been calculated under the assumption that the pulse broadening from
the scattering is all due to this new screen, yielding $1.24^{+0.26}_{-0.25}$
cm$^{-3}$. Further studies of this system will allow further investigation of
the timescales of scattering and the properties of the medium.

waveform generative model named
Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) is proposed to improve the limited pitch
controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features are outside the $F_{0}$ range observed
in the training data. To address this problem, QPNet with two novel designs is
proposed. First, the PDCNN component is applied to dynamically change the
network architecture of WN according to the given auxiliary $F_{0}$ features.
Second, a cascaded network structure is utilized to simultaneously model the
long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

geometry, but that could have a high distortion in the case of embedding graphs
with scale-free or hierarchical structure. Recently, some GCNs are proposed to
deal with this problem in non-Euclidean geometry, e.g., hyperbolic geometry.
Although hyperbolic GCNs achieve promising performance, existing hyperbolic
graph operations actually cannot rigorously follow the hyperbolic geometry,
which may limit the ability of hyperbolic geometry and thus hurt the
performance of hyperbolic GCNs. In this paper, we propose a novel hyperbolic
GCN named Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which rigorously
guarantees the learned node features follow the hyperbolic geometry.
Specifically, we rebuild the graph operations of hyperbolic GCNs with
Lorentzian version, e.g., the feature transformation and non-linear activation.
Also, an elegant neighborhood aggregation method is designed based on the
centroid of Lorentzian distance. Moreover, we prove some proposed graph
operations are equivalent in different types of hyperbolic geometry, which
fundamentally indicates their correctness. Experiments on six datasets show
that LGCN performs better than the state-of-the-art methods. LGCN has lower
distortion to learn the representation of tree-likeness graphs and thus is more
efficient. LGCN also has lower overfitting risk due to the unique geometry of
hyperbolic space. LGCN is general to handle different types of edge in the graph
and can be combined with other effective GCN architectures. Moreover, LGCN
produces the embedding in hyperbolic space, which is convenient for visualizing
high-dimensional graphs. The code of this paper is available at:

impulsivity, which reflects the change in individual behavior due to group

effective framework to explore delay discounting in a system of organisms.

scattering problems. The main focus is on plane waves scattered by smoothly
varying material inhomogeneities. The proposed method works for any frequency
$\omega$, but is especially efficient for high-frequency problems. It is based
on the fact that the solution $\mathbf{u}(\omega)$ can be approximated by
$\Re\left(\mathbf{u}(\omega/2)+i\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega/2}\right)$, where
$\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\omega/2}$ is a small perturbation velocity field that can
be computed by solving a sequence of simpler problems at half the frequency.
The perturbation velocity is given by a linear combination of divergence-free
vector fields, and the coefficients are determined by solving a linear system
for real and imaginary parts separately. The key advantage of this method over
other high-frequency approaches is that it does not introduce any
approximations: the proposed method can be viewed as an efficient implementation
of the Born approximation for scalar waves. Furthermore, the method is extended
to wavefields propagating in several directions. The advantages of the method
are demonstrated for several material inhomogeneities with different shapes and
sizes.
  The main ideas behind the algorithm are general and can be applied to other
wave types (e.g., elastic waves) and wavefield expansions (e.g., finite
difference).

  The program consists of several modules:
  -- ViDaStats: implements main statistical algorithms;

2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we develop a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as inaccurate due to the large Lebesgue spaces required to achieve
high order accuracy. However, in the case of Newtonian potentials, the
associated error analysis involves only $L_\infty$ spaces, and thus requires
significantly fewer functions of smoothness. We demonstrate the performance of
our algorithm over a variety of complicated domains.
